overview.text: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is an aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride, a gas; it is an inorganic, strong acid. In water, HCl dissociates essentially completely into hydronium and chloride ions, which explains its “strong acid” classification—strength refers to ionization, not simply how concentrated a sample is. In the body, gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid as part of stomach acid, which helps digestion alongside enzymes. Beyond biology, it is an important industrial chemical: uses include cleaning oxide from steel (“pickling”), processing ores, producing other chemicals, and adjusting water pH. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive, so laboratory and industrial use requires appropriate controls.

key_facts.text: Hydrochloric acid is hydrogen chloride dissolved in water; hydrogen chloride itself is a gas.
In aqueous solution, HCl is a strong acid because it dissociates essentially completely, forming hydronium and chloride ions.
Gastric parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid; stomach acid and enzymes help break down food, including proteins.
Industrial uses include steel pickling, ore processing, chemical production, and pH adjustment in water treatment.
Hydrochloric acid is corrosive and can damage tissues, so it must be handled with appropriate safety precautions.
